title: Notes of Ministry - 10 - September 1973

source.file: Various/Notes of Ministry - 10 - September (2034)/Notes of Ministry - 10 - Septem - Various.epub

paragraphs.text: I have been impressed, beloved brethren, to say a word about the life of the christian. It is not a matter on which I could or would seek to lecture anybody, it is a subject in the knowledge of which I myself would be glad to grow; but even as thinking of oneself and observing others I believe that the Lord would ask us what is the quality of our life as christians. There are many believers who cling to a long-established belief in Christ; they accepted Him as their Saviour a very long time ago. I remember once preaching on the subject of repentance and being spoken to by a sister afterwards who said to me, ‘They must be terrible people where you came from—I repented years ago’. You can see where her present life was not.

Many cling to a place and part in some particular circle or company and go on as if the mere presence at, and to some extent belonging to, such a company was sufficient for the life of a christian. Many there have been, and I trust are not now, who even seemed to think that the life of the christian lay in inheritance and in that their fathers and grandfathers were believers and devout and godly men, and that their life was in some sense an overspill from the life of the previous generation; but this is not so.

The life of the christian lies in what is current to the christian in his own day and a christian is not one in whom things are dead or moribund or quiescent. A christian is one in whom there is a well of water springing up into eternal life. The absence of vitality and vigour in some believers is, I think, very much due to the shallowness of their appreciation of Christ as Saviour and that in itself springs from shallowness in their apprehension of their need of Him as a Saviour. It is not for nothing that it is often observable that those who in some sense, as most people would acknowledge, have a great deal to repent of, are found afterwards as the most vigorous and energetic and lively of christians. I think the woman of whom it was said “Her many sins are forgiven” (Luke 7: 47) went away from that occasion living Christ, whereas ones who thought that they had not much to be forgiven would go away with a sense that they had not particularly been set forward.

It is not that in any sense we charge one another with sin, or with a history of sin—I trust that that kind of thing is over—but each knows his own heart and, as the Scripture says, each knows “the plague of his own heart” (1 Kings 8: 38). Each knows the quality and character of the order of life and activity and conduct from which the death of Christ has saved him, which death has been necessary if he was to be saved at all. Each knows that, each has had to come to Christ himself to find salvation and the power of salvation working as available for him and therefore effective in him. It is the apprehension in, the soul of the majesty of God which produces that conviction of the need of Christ as Saviour which establishes something in the soul that is firm and, if I may use the word, powerful.

Therefore the first essential—if there is to be life of the quality that Paul is speaking about in these two scriptures—is some apprehension of the greatness of who God is and of what His demands in relation to men righteously are. The apprehension of what God is in perfection of righteousness and holiness, being “of purer eyes than to behold evil”

(Habakkuk l: 13), brings upon man the challenge of what his own life before God is, if he is brought before God as One who has a right to assert things in relation to the qualities of His own character and nature. If man as a sinner is brought before God whose standard is only perfect holiness and righteousness, the more, the deeper, the apprehension the soul has of who God is in those distinguishing qualities, the deeper will be his apprehension of his need of that which will satisfy God. In a certain sense the more the terror of the Lord, by which Paul would persuade men, is known in the soul as bearing on it as brought before God as the One who in the end has the right to judge, the deeper will be the sense of apprehension in love of the One who has borne everything in order that that judgment might not fall upon oneself.

Therefore I say that the initial steps in the quality of the life of the christian depend on his apprehension, even as a sinner, of the greatness of God and God’s abhorrence of sin, and therefore of His abhorrence of sin as known in men and women; and the more that abhorrence on God’s part is apprehended the more there will be the sense of thankfulness and appreciation of the One who has borne the judgment that otherwise would fall on me as a sinner, to make me fit for the presence of such a God as that. In the cry of a man who says,

“O God, have compassion on me, the sinner” (Luke 18: 13), there is the foundation of the life of a convicted christian who will be here in testimony, a man who can go down to his house justified and by his life will justify the salvation that is his.

The sense of “Lord, save me. And immediately Jesus stretched out his hand” (Matthew 14: 31, 32), is the foundation of a life which is powerful for God—as Paul says, “powerful according to God” (2 Corinthians 10: 4)—the foundation of a life such as that is found in one who has an apprehension of what God is and therefore of what He may require from man and what He may demand, even of the sinner. If God demands what is required of the sinner, the sinner will find that the wages of sin is death, and God has a right to require that penalty from the sinner. But, on the other hand, He has provided that which will relieve the sinner from judgment and give him the liberty to be before God according to what man ought to be for God.

The sense of relief in the soul, and affection for the One who has provided the means by which iniquity may be taken away and sins may be atoned for—the sense in which such a one is apprehended lays the basis for a quality of christian life which is not intended to be given up. The sorrowful thing with many of us is that we have had experiences in conversion, perhaps many years ago, and we have allowed the accumulation of time and of experience to overlay the freshness and the vitality which belonged to us in that day. The Lord would, I am sure, speak to us to revive us so that there may be a quality in our christian life now which corresponds to that of which Paul is speaking here.

Paul is not boasting in these scriptures; he is not saying, I will tell you what a good christian I am, but, This is what is normal to me; this is not something I have put on for the occasion, this is something that is normal to me, that “I live by faith … of the Son of God” and “for me to live is Christ”.

One reflects on these things, beloved, not in any sense critically of other people, but critically of oneself, because I feel that there is a need in the present day of our being here in the vitality of life, that is not only a testimony to others but is the only real source of satisfaction to ourselves. The sense of being here as a person who ought to be living as a christian and is not, is one of the most self-defeating experiences that men and women can have. The sense of being a kind of failed christian is one of the most disheartening experiences that a soul can have. The sense of being here in the vitality of “for me to live is Christ” is one of the most uplifting and edifying experiences that any man or woman can have or be sustained in.

Therefore, beloved, the Lord would appeal to us, just a few of us here this afternoon, young and old. Perhaps we here embrace as wide a range of age as you would find in any gathering of people on a Lord’s day, but “for me to live is Christ” is open to any of us, and I think the Lord would appeal to us as to whether we are prepared to be here on this basis. In Philippians Paul gives no reason for what he says, in Galatians he does, “I live by faith, the faith of the Son of God, who has loved me and given himself for me”. This goes back to what I was saying, that it is the apprehension in the soul of the fact that the Son of God has given Himself for us where otherwise God would have had to demand from us, ourselves, the penalty that our sins and the state of our lives demands as before Him. The Son of God loves him, not only loved him, but loves him and gave himself for him.

We would find, even in human things, that if, for instance, a man is in danger of drowning and someone plunges in and rescues him, for ever afterwards his life is characterised by gratitude to the man who rescued him from such a fate. If the man who had rescued him was spoken ill of he would rise up in his defence. If the man who had rescued him was forgotten he would see that people were reminded of him. How much more then with Jesus!

It is not that He rescued you from drowning, but He saved you from the judgment of God. If He is ill spoken of, do you rise up in His defence? If you do not, you cannot say, “For me to live is Christ”. If He is forgotten, do you remember Him and see that He is remembered? If you do not, you cannot say, “For me to live is Christ.”

The Lord would impress us I think this afternoon with the essentiality of being stimulated in the fact that the Son of God loves us still and He delivered Himself up for us. He is not delivering Himself up for us still, that is a work that He did once, and once for all. It not only does not need to be repeated but cannot be repeated. He cannot come back into the conditions in which He laid down His life as a Man and give Himself again. It is a work that has not only been done once for all but it cannot be repeated. But it was done, and thank God it was done, and thank the Lord Himself that He was willing to do this, not only for God but for you and me, in order that there might be a basis laid for God on which sin could be taken out of the way. So Paul had a lively sense in his own soul that the Son of God did this for him.
There is a hymn that says—

‘Teach me that if none other had sinned but I alone—
Yet still, Thy blood, Lord Jesus, Thine only, must atone’

If there had been only Paul who was a sinner then the Son of God would have had to deliver Himself up for him. And if there had only been me, or if there had only been you, He would have had to deliver Himself up for me or for you, and He has done it. You and I know that we were not the only sinners there had ever been, but we cannot procure salvation for anybody else; each obtains it for himself by faith in the Son of God who did this for him.

You go back again to the illustrations of those who have made sacrifices in order to secure and preserve the lives of others and you come back to this, ‘Am I still kept in the lively sense of responsive love to Him who gave Himself for me, or has love grown cold in me?’
You go round the towns and villages in England and in nearly all of them you will see war memorials and on them the names of the local men who died during wars for the country.

Sometimes they put texts on them—sometimes they put, ‘They gave themselves that we might live’. When these monuments were first put up, some of them now fifty-five years ago, and some of them about twenty-five years ago, people were warm in their remembrance.

They thought how devoted these men had been, and what a sorrowful thing it was if anyone forgot them. I can well remember when, on the day on which the end of the war was remembered, and therefore the deaths of the men who died in it were remembered, all the traffic stopped. Men would stop their cars and get out and stand by them for two minutes in order that there might be a manifestation of remembrance of those who sacrificed themselves for others. Does that happen now? Have any of you boys ever seen that happen on Remembrance Day in November? Have you ever seen a man stop what he was doing to remember those who died for their country? I am not saying whether they should or whether they should not, what I am drawing out is the change that there has been, and it is the same in relation to the Lord Jesus.

Immediately after His death, as we can see in the book of the Acts, He was warmly remembered by those who knew He had given Himself for them, and as you come down to the present day you find it is as it says in the psalm, “I am forgotten in their heart as a dead man” (Psalm 31: 12). Not with Paul, “I live by faith”; “For me to live is Christ, and to die gain”. I am not talking this afternoon about dying. Paul says, “To die gain”, but Paul also says, “But if to live in flesh is my lot, this is for me worth the while”. Why is it worth while? Because “for me to live is Christ”—that is why it is worth while. Many believers you have to take account of, many professing christians, then you have to say to them, ‘Is it worth while?’ I look at you and I say, ‘Is it worth while?’ and you look at me and you say to me, ‘Well, I look at you, are you a manifestation that it is worth while?’ But it was worth while for Paul, “For me to live is Christ”.

We are tested as we grow older as to these things and as to how much Christ is now a reality to us. Often when we are young we are fresh in the remembrance of the Lord Jesus. Some preaching or some preacher has made an impression on our soul and we are lively in the sense that He died for me and I will live for Him—and there are few things more attractive than a young christian who is set to be here for the Son of God. And we grow old, and we look back over our days, and we find that things have grown cold and have diminished. There is another hymn that says, ‘Through many a deed of shame, we learn that love grows cold’.

Love grows cold, and the Lord may lay us aside. He may do any different thing with us. He may ensure by one means or another that we have a time in which we are tested as to whether Christ is our life, or whether something else is, or whether nothing is.

It is a sorrowful thing to meet anybody that is really old and find that you could not say that Christ is their life. You could not say that the world was their life, perhaps you could not say anything more than that they themselves were their life. But, beloved, we are tested as we grow old and the only way for a christian to grow old is “For me to live is Christ”—it is the only possible way. We have spent a long time and life goes very, very quickly. I do not know whether it is a sign of growing older oneself, but life seems to go quicker every week. The only way for a christian to live is, “For me to live is Christ”. It is the only way to get substance into the day.

There is a great deal of occupation, and necessary occupation, and there is a great deal that is done and done well. The question for us all, beloved, the question for me, is whether in all the doing Christ is my life. “For me to live is Christ, and to die gain”. Well, it only means that what is being experienced in the Spirit becomes actuality. “But if to live in flesh is my lot, this is for me worth the while”—it is a great thing as you grow older, however old you are, however young you are—every ono of us is growing older at exactly the same rate. Think of that when you are young; you think of old people and you say they get older and older; you are getting older at exactly the same rate. If you continue in the flesh, is it worth the while, or would something else be more worth the while? If Christ is not your life something else would certainly seem worth the while in your life. You may ask me what are the evidences of it, what are the tokens of it? I think we can test ourselves by what our minds and hearts and thoughts revert to when we are otherwise unoccupied. If you have nothing else to do, what do you do? Do you pick up something that belongs to the present course of things, or do you pick up something that relates to the course of things that is soon going to fill the world with His glory? That is the way, that is the token, that “For me to live is Christ”.

If you talk to somebody, does His name ever enter into your conversation? If “For me to live is Christ” is true of you it will never be left out. If you write a letter do people look in vain for some impression about the Lord Jesus? Do not forget, you profess to be a christian, you profess to owe everything to the Lord Jesus. If you speak, or if you write a letter, is He there, is He in it, is He mentioned in it, is He demonstrated in it? “For me to live is Christ”. He would have Himself demonstrated in everything that we do. Is any service done? For whose glory? For His? “For me to live is Christ”. Are the saints cared for? If “For me to live is Christ” is true of us, they will be cared for as He would care for them. Is sacrifice called for? He sacrificed everything and if “For me to live is Christ” is true, that same sacrificial spirit will mark you and me.

It does not exactly call for our dying. It may call for our laying down our lives, which is a very different thing. There is another hymn—these things seem to come back to my mind—that used to say this—‘Teach me to live, ‘twere easier far to die’. There are many people who can die and look forward to being with Christ whose life would be given a very different character if they found that to live was Christ at the present time.

Well, beloved, I just leave these impressions with the brethren, I do not want to be very long, I would sooner leave an impression than say a lot. I think that is what any preacher ought to be able to do; to leave an impression rather than say a lot. But I believe that the Lord would search us in the present position in which we are identified with the testimony as to whether there is a quality of life in us which is a testimony in itself. You may say, ‘Well, the pathway of separation does not leave much room for manifesting this to others’. A pathway of separation is the essential basis for manifesting christianity to other people. You do not manifest the truth of christianity to others by being one with them in everything that they do. Christianity belongs to a rejected Man and its truth is always compromised when rejection is surrendered. And rejection by the world and its order of things is a key that opens the door for us to find that “For me to live is Christ”.
“I live by faith”. Paul says. You have to live by faith. You cannot see Him at the present time.

He will soon appear and every eye shall see Him. For the moment we live by faith and if we live by faith we live by piety. A pious life is one in which “For me to live is Christ”. Piety is often defined by us as bringing God into all our circumstances, but piety actually is manifesting God in all our circumstances, and you do not manifest God unless Christ is your life.

Well, beloved, I just leave these impressions with the brethren. They have come to me during the day and I pass them on as much to myself as to others. Our brother prayed that the preacher might find the word was for him as much as to anybody else, and that would be true.

One wonders as we go on day by day how more really we can make it true that Christ is our life, and “For me to live is Christ”. It does not mean giving up all your other work and all your other occupations, it does not mean that you just retire into being a recluse and a meditative, but what it does is to bring some transforming power into everything else that you do, every conversation, every word spoken, every activity done, something new is brought into them if “For me to live is Christ”.
I think He would revive us in this and may He do so for His name’s sake.

These passages would bear on the way that the experience of headship is worked out in conditions of outward obscurity. It is a feature of the glory of God that He chooses to do things in a way which, as far as men are concerned, is hidden. Man does not understand it or welcome it. His brethren reproachfully said to Jesus, “No one does anything in secret and himself seeks to be known in public” (John 7: 4). “Manifest thyself”, they said, but the Lord Jesus did not do things that way. He moved into every situation when the Father’s will directed it, not according to the way that the reasoning of man would have operated to bring about human greatness and glory.

It is a feature of the glorious way in which He acts as Head, that what is hidden is in fact being developed to expand into a universe of glory. The universe of glory stands directly related to the Babe in the manger. What could there be more outwardly small and obscure than Jesus wrapped in swaddling clothes and laid in a manger? And yet think, beloved, of the expansion of that in moral and spiritual glory into a whole universe where everything that hath breath is going to praise God.

But the working out of it means that we have to face what is involved in conditions of obscurity, maybe famine. There was famine where we read in Elijah’s day and it was at his word. He said to Ahab, “There shall not be dew nor rain these years, except by my word”.

Not just that there was not going to be any rain, but neither dew nor rain, as though men would have to prove in detailed experience morning by morning that even the dew had stopped because God had not been served aright.

Then Elijah has to be tested in his own spiritual being as to what this word is going to mean, so he is told by God to go and to hide himself by the torrent Cherith. God commanded the ravens and there was a complete reversal of the natural order of things so that ravens fed a man; that was God’s command and the ravens had to be subject. Every creature of God is subject to God. The cattle upon a thousand hills are all subject to God. God brings them under tribute to the saints as the occasion needs. So the ravens here are commanded to feed Elijah in this hidden position and then the torrent dries up. Elijah was being freshly tested as to his own word. He is told to go to Zarephath, to the widow that God had commanded to maintain him. It is of interest that God should choose that this widow woman should be at Zarephath by Zidon. In the Lord’s time the Syrophoenician woman came from the parts of Tyre and Sidon. I suppose there would be a moral link of faith between those two women.

Elijah was a man who was subject, we might say, to headship and he immediately brings in the test as to headship. The woman is subject to his direction. There had been no rain in the land, but he asks for a little water and she goes to fetch it. The test becomes intensified as he says, “Bring me, I pray thee, a morsel of bread in thy hand”. The whole sorrowful position opens out, but that does not deter Elijah from asserting the claims of headship. So he says, “Make me first” that is the claim of headship. It is similar to the word in Colossians 1: 18—“That He might have the first place in all things”. Well, beloved, has Christ the first place in all things? We have been speaking together of the glorious greatness of Jesus as Head, but how do we fare when the word of Jehovah comes to us in testing challenge; when all that is in mind is just to gather two sticks and eat and die?

Elijah was not unsympathetic with this woman’s exercises. Do not think that the Lord is unsympathetic. He knows the reality of obscure conditions. He knows what the heart of man according to the flesh would like by way of human greatness; but He puts that all on one side and He says, ‘I want you to give me the first place’. Well, this was a test for this woman; she was facing, literally, death and she has this request from a person who had suddenly appeared. She knew he had a link with God and she must have had some sense of having been commanded of God to maintain Elijah. Now this test comes as to whether she is prepared to make available to him what stood between her and death for herself and her son.

The Spirit brings “the first place” in in Colossians in relation to Jesus being Firstborn from among the dead. That is the setting, I think, in which the Spirit would always exert with us the claims of Jesus as Head; that is, we are having to do with Him in a great area of things where death and the grave have been eternally conquered and where we have to do with the God to whom nothing is impossible, suppose Abraham of old would be linked with this woman in the spirit of his being when he came into the truth of the Almighty God, that is the God who raises the dead.

So here she was, she was facing death, and the challenge comes, “Make me thereof a little cake first”. Well, she had not got much—and yet what there was! A little like the disciples when they thought that five loaves and two small fishes were not very much, but under the power of Christ in headship what expansion there was—thousands of persons fed as the loaves and fishes were made available to the hand of Jesus, the Almighty God. Well, what was it this woman had? She had a handful of meal in a barrel. Outwardly not very great, just a barrel and not very much in the barrel, just a handful. A handful is something that can be easily encompassed. It is not exactly the windows of heaven being opened in blessing, that was to come later.

What fulness there is as we seek help from the Spirit to get a handful of meal in relation to the life of Jesus. What handfuls of meal, we might say, there are in the four gospels. Another has rightly said, ‘strong meat’, yet a handful of meal is always available to us. It would link on with the manna as coming in at the beginning of the day, but it is always available all through the day. When some fresh test comes in as to the headship of Christ, as to whether we are prepared to give Him the first place in all things, what is available to us? A handful of meal, so that we feed on the One who was meek and lowly in heart.

It has been said that meekness is towards men and lowliness is towards God. God intended that this handful of meal should be constantly maintained. It lies behind all the ordinances as to the oblation. I think it is particularly enjoyed by those who are maintained in the spirit of an overcomer, so that to one of the overcomers the promise of the Lord was that he would be given to eat of the hidden manna. Mr. Coates referred to this as being some impression of the delight that God had in the life of Jesus.

Then there is the little oil in a cruse; the availability of the Spirit of God, despised by man but increasingly valued by believers on the Lord Jesus. Where would we be if the Spirit were not here? The Lord went back to heaven and after those ten days of waiting the Spirit came down. A body had been prepared for Jesus, but a dwelling place for the Spirit of God had been prepared by Jesus in the hearts of the disciples—the sound out of heaven filled the house (Acts 2: 2).

So what expansion there is as we connect the meal with Jesus and the oil with the Spirit. To the believer there is an opening up into a realm where God Himself is known. The service of God is re-established, when the twelve stones are taken and the altar built (1 Kings 18: 32).

The pitchers of water being emptied one after the other on the altar would intensify our feelings as to what Jesus has suffered that a universe for God might he secured. Feeding on the humanity of Jesus, and depending on the blessed Spirit of truth, strengthens us so that we can go through in assurance for a whole year, that is, for the rest of the days of this dispensation. The word of God stands that the handful of meal in the barrel is not going to waste, nor is the oil in the cruse going to fail.
What a sense we have, beloved, of being under the control of Christ who has given us His own personal assurance that He is going to carry things through until the completion of the age.

In Exodus 2 the circumstances were, of course, a marriage in the Lord, and then a child, a son, is born who is later called Moses. He is valued by the woman as being fair. Acts and Hebrews bring the father into it, or both the parents, but here it is the woman’s valuation and she hides him; she hides him in the house first, I take it, for three months, then she hides him in this ark of reeds. It is the same word, according to the note, as Noah’s ark, so there would be a link, no doubt, between this ark placed in the sedge on the bank of the river and the ark of Noah as facing the waters of judgment, and the child is preserved as Noah was preserved in the ark.

This would be preparation in view of reaching through to the discernment of headship so as to be available for service. Moses, of course, was distinctive, but what God does in a distinctive servant is a model for all. As we said in the reading, it is not a time when we would look for outstanding gift, although we would look for gift. I think we would be right, and would be with the Lord, in looking for gift, younger persons being raised up, and maybe older persons being liberated, persons being raised up who can serve the brethren and can serve men.

But the main point is being devoted to the saints for service; I think that is how we might think of Moses in this setting. The house of Stephanas in Corinth was not devoted to service—never let us have service as the object, that is the highway to disaster—but devoted to the saints for service. But that means a hidden preparation, facing obscurity.

You might say this would bear on household baptism. Yes, thank God for the truth as to household baptism. Do not let us think it is something that has always been understood. The Spirit of truth had to assert that it was not a matter of the baptism of infants, but of persons as members of households, because in the preaching of the gospel, whether as it came to the Gentiles through Peter in Cornelius’ house, or through Paul to the Gentile jailor, the word in both cases is, “Thou shalt be saved, thou and thy house” (Acts 11: 14 and 16: 31).

The Spirit would teach us lessons from the ark being placed in the sedge and not in the middle of the river. Let us remember that in 1937 Mr. Taylor said that universities were becoming traps for the people of God (N.S. Vol. 84, p.386). Oh, do not let the young people be placed in the middle of the river, in universities. That is not the line of preservation.

Preservation means that we keep as far away from the current of the world as we can. The higher you get up in the world, the nearer you get to the god of it, and what a god he is! A god that will allure persons to destruction, whereas the line of headship would attract persons into life.

Let us understand for ourselves, and all our young people, that the line of preservation to keep away from the main stream of the world’s independency and to be content to be in a safe ark. She was careful, this beloved woman; she would represent the spirit of motherhood in the assembly as she plastered the ark with resin and with pitch. And then the sister was there to see what was going to happen. God’s hand was over it all, of course, and over Moses.

The preparation went on. Think of those forty years in Pharaoh’s court. Moses was not spoilt, because at the end of that he did not aspire to the throne; he went out to see how his brethren were getting on. He had a desire to serve the people of God, a sense that the reproach of the Christ was greater riches than the treasures of Egypt, and what wealth there was at that time!
You might say he had within his grasp the supreme position in this world and he put it all on one side and went and spent forty years in the wilderness.

He was not ready after those first forty years. Do let not us think that, when we have been through a certain course of experience, our training has been completed. Maybe we have to have some time in Arabia, but let us learn God in it all, for in christianity we do not have to wait as Moses did; we can begin serving the brethren at once and as we serve them we learn in obscurity with God to serve them better.

It has often been said that placing footstools in the meeting room in the right places is one way in which the saints are served; often a hidden service, the footstools are just there, and nobody perhaps enquires how they got there, but somebody put them in the right place. Let us learn to serve the saints in detail, but as we want to serve them more it means we have to be developed in our secret soul history with God and learn more of the greatness of Christ as the One who did not come to be ministered unto but to minister. What a Servant He was! Let us catch something of the spirit of our Master; as we serve Him, we shall know how to serve the saints.

Mary caught something of the spirit of this where we read in John 12. The setting here no doubt would be what is presented as Paul writes to those beloved brethren at Colosse. This was not the Lord’s supper. The Lord prepares that for us. This is where lovers prepare Him a supper. They made Him a supper, and Mary is available with this pound of ointment of pure nard of great price. They made Him a supper; that would involve the recognition of Christ in headship as having the first place. Mary is not here, as we might gather from other gospels, with an alabaster flask, for the vessel here was herself. She contained this measured amount, this pound of ointment, and she made it available in herself with a sensitive understanding of what was in view in the Lord’s movements.

Another has pointed out that no one else there really understood what was involved, although the Lord had constantly taught them that He was going on to be killed. No one else except Mary understood the trend of things, but she understood that the only end to what was happening was burial for Jesus, and she brings this ointment in view of the day of His burial.
How it appealed to the Lord, what it meant to the Lord, just this touch of entering sensitively into His own feelings!
Do we have that power by the Spirit to enter sensitively into the Lord’s feelings at any time?

Mary was available at this time as a suited vessel with just what was needed by way of appreciation of Christ personally, and it filled the house. As the Spirit came down from heaven the sound filled the house, but this is ointment from one woman, one sister, representing the subjective features of the work of God in the saints.

Are we ready for that at any time, when something is on hand, especially in the assembly? Are we available as sensitive to the feelings of headship so that we can bring in just what is needed to minister first to the heart of Christ, and then, by way of enlargement, refreshment and encouragement to those who love Jesus? There was the voice of criticism, but the Spirit of God just refers to it, so that we are warned, and then passes on.

So we need not make much of interruptions or attempted diversions, because God is never really diverted. He is never hindered in any thought of His, so we can be assured that the power and resources of Christ as Head, and the availability of the blessed Spirit in support here, are going to continue until that moment when we shall hear the assembling shout of the Lord Jesus and we shall see Him face to face. What a moment that will be! The waiting time is to prepare us for it, and to help us to be available now for Himself in His gracious influence over us so that we may help those who desire to be here for the glory of God. So this great, divine system that we were speaking of is extended as God has His own way in the hearts of men. May the Lord bless the word!

DIVINE BLESSING—In Ephesians 1: 3 we are spoken of as “blessed … with every spiritual blessing in the heavenlies in Christ”. One had not noted sufficiently the bearing of the preposition “with”. The sense is that these rich blessings have not just been placed upon us, but they involve that the believer is marked characteristically by something of the power and value of them. That must relate to the inward working of the Holy Spirit. How great this matter is; not only that we are so blessed, but that the Father has before Him those who are formed, substantially in accordance with what has been conferred upon them, and are thus able to respond richly to Him.

VALUING THE PROPHETIC WORD—After receiving the prophetic word from Nathan, David “went in and sat before Jehovah” (2 Samuel 7: 18). He is an example for us. If a word of prophecy comes to us—perhaps in a meeting for ministry, or in the reading of the scriptures—let us go in and sit before God. Let us reflect before Him on what He has said.
Let our hearts go out to Him in fresh response .in answer to some impression of His glory, some fresh touch as to His purposes and His ways, and the One in whom they all centre.

David here has profound impressions of the sovereign workings of God “for thy word’s sake, and according to thine own heart” (2 Samuel 7: 21). He reviews the ways of God from Egypt onward and rises in a spirit of worship to God as the Same (see footnote to 2 Samuel 7: 28, in the Darby Translation).
